I want to create a docs site that we'll publish to help explain Frame Job features. Create a new astro
  Starlight site in a folder in the repo. See docs: https://starlight.astro.build/. Then create an exhaustive list of all features, and create documentation pages for them.
<skill-format>true</skill-format>

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.
I'll start by scouting what exists: the current user guide, the toolchain, and Starlight's current setup.

# Frame Job User Guide Frame Job is a native macOS video editor for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 26 or later. You open a movie, arrange it on layered tracks over a fixed canvas, then trim, cut, grade, caption, animate and export it. Every edit you make in the window can also be made by an AI agent over MCP, or by the built-in Assistant. The quickest way in: **File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) on a movie makes an untitled project sized and timed to it, with the movie on Track 1, ready to cut. Save writes a `.framejob` package. ## The pages Read the first four in order to learn the editor; the rest stand alone. 1. [Projects and media](projects-and-media.md) — starting, saving and opening projects, the `.framejob` package, the Document tab's canvas settings, importing files, the Media tab and relinking. 2. [The timeline and playback](timeline.md) — the editor window, tracks and their switches, the ruler and playhead, zoom, selection, snapping, markers, the in/out range and playback. 3. [Editing clips](editing.md) — placing, moving, trimming, slipping, splitting, deleting and closing gaps, copy and paste, and nests. 4. [Canvas, layers, text and shapes](canvas-and-layers.md) — placing a picture on the canvas, opacity, blend modes, shadows and filters, text, shape, image and background clips, and matte tracks. 5. [Motion, actions and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md) — actions that animate a clip's properties over time, motion presets, and transitions between clips. 6. [Speed, reverse and freeze frames](speed.md) — constant speed, fitting a clip to a length, rate stretch, speed ramps and their presets, reversing and freeze frames. 7. [Audio](audio.md) — clip levels, fades and their shapes, ducking by clip length or by speech, noise reduction, compression, pan, mute and solo, Normalize and Synchronize Audio. 8. [Remove Silences and Remove Filler Words](cleanup-tools.md) — cutting dead air and filler words out of a spoken recording in one step. 9. [Captions and transcription](captions.md) — importing and exporting captions, and transcribing speech on this Mac or with AssemblyAI into subtitles or word-by-word captions. 10. [The Transcript](transcript.md) — reading what is said in the project as text in the inspector, following it as the video plays, and clicking a word to jump there. 11. [Colour grading](color-grading.md) — the Color tab, wheels, curves, looks and LUTs, adjustment clips and qualifiers, Show Ungraded and the scopes. 12. [HDR and colour management](hdr-and-color.md) — how sources are read, camera log, SDR and HDR (HLG) projects, blending, and HDR and SDR deliverables. 13. [Motion graphics](graphics.md) — graphic clips, the built-in graphics, their properties in the inspector, and bringing in your own. 14. [Vertical and framing](vertical-and-framing.md) — the faces, people and salient regions Frame Job finds in a clip's picture on this Mac, View ▸ Show Subjects, Clip ▸ Follow Subject…, which frames the selected clips on them for a vertical or square canvas, and File ▸ Make Vertical Version…, which makes the whole timeline's 9:16, 4:5 or 1:1 version. 15. [Podcasts and several cameras](multicam.md) — cameras on tracks of their own, a program track cut from them, Clip ▸ Switch by Speaker… to cut it from the microphones, and Clip ▸ Switch Angle ▸ to re-pick one shot from another camera. 16. [Screen recording](screen-recording.md) — recording a display or a window with system audio, microphone and click rings, recording a camera on its own or beside the screen, and recording voice-overs. 17. [Exporting](export.md) — the export sheet, its formats and settings, presets, the Export Queue, and saving single frames. 18. [The Assistant](assistant.md) — chatting with Claude in the inspector to edit the open project, on your own Anthropic key. 19. [Driving Frame Job from an AI agent (MCP)](mcp.md) — connecting an MCP client such as Claude Code, how calls behave, and every tool. 20. [Settings](settings.md) — the Settings window, updates (Check for Updates… in the downloaded copy), the View choices Frame Job remembers, and where it keeps its files. 21. [Menus and keyboard shortcuts](menus-and-shortcuts.md) — every menu command with its shortcut, and the keys, gestures and context menus that have no menu item. Writing your own graphic module is covered by the [graphics API reference](../graphics-api.md). ------- # Podcasts and several cameras A show filmed with more than one camera — a podcast with a camera on each guest, an interview with a wide and a close shot — is cut in Frame Job as ordinary clips on ordinary tracks. There is no special multicam clip: each camera is a track, and the edit you watch is a **program track** in front of them, made of pieces copied from whichever camera you want at each moment. ## Setting it up 1. Put each camera's recording on a track of its own, lined up in time. **Clip ▸ Synchronize Audio** lines the selected recordings up by their sound ([Audio](audio.md)). Name each track after its camera (double-click the track's header): the names are what Switch Angle lists. 2. Add a track in front of them for the program, and put the first shots on it. An agent does this with `copy_pieces` (below); by hand, copy a camera's clip onto the program track and cut it with **Clip ▸ Split** (⌘T). The camera tracks stay underneath. They can stay shown — the program track is in front and covers them — or be hidden with their track switch; a hidden track's clips still count as an angle. ## Switch by Speaker **Clip ▸ Switch by Speaker…** cuts a whole program track for you from a conversation: it watches each person's microphone and shows whoever is talking. Do it in this order: 1. **Synchronize Audio first** (Setting it up, above). Switch by Speaker trusts where the clips sit and does not check that they are in sync, so a camera moved or slipped afterwards — with **Clip ▸ Slip** or by dragging it — puts its shots out of step with the voices. 2. Select every camera's clips and every microphone's clips, then choose **Clip ▸ Switch by Speaker…**. It is offered when the selection holds clips with a picture on two or more tracks (each such track is a camera, up to nine) and at least one clip with its sound on. 3. Afterwards, fix single shots with **Switch Angle** (below) and move cuts with an ordinary roll. **Which tracks are microphones.** By default, every track holding a selected clip with sound and no picture — a separate recording from a microphone or a recorder. When nothing like that is selected, each camera's own sound is its microphone. A camera's sound detached with **Clip ▸ Detach Audio** is never picked by default; you can choose it in a Microphone pop-up. A camera clip that is still linked to its detached sound cannot be switched: the sheet says so and names the clip, and **Clip ▸ Attach Audio** puts the two back together first. **The sheet.** One row per person: a Microphone pop-up and the Camera that shows them, paired front to back to start with. Then: - **Wide** — the camera shown when nobody or everybody talks; a camera no person uses is picked to start with when exactly one is left over, else None. - **Minimum shot** (2 s) — a shorter shot is merged into its neighbour. - **Cut** (0.2 s before speech) — how long before a new speaker's first word the cut comes. - **Crosstalk shows** — the Wide, or holds the Current speaker, while two talk at once for a second or more. - **Ignore bleed** (15 dB below a speaker's own level) — every microphone also -------

Open a movie, arrange it on layered tracks over a fixed canvas, then trim, cut, grade, caption, animate and export it. Every edit you make in the window can also be made by an AI agent over MCP, or by the built-in Assistant, and each one is an ordinary undo step. Apple Silicon, macOS 26 or later. # New Project Setup Skill

Provides standardized configuration templates and preferences for setting up new projects. Use this skill when creating new projects to ensure consistent tooling and configuration.

---

## Default Stack Preferences

Unless otherwise specified by the user:

1. **Language**: TypeScript
2. **Package Manager**: pnpm
3. **Code Formatting**: Prettier

---

## TypeScript Configuration

When setting up TypeScript projects, use these compiler options as defaults. These represent preferred strictness, module setup, and resolution settings.

### Base tsconfig.json Template

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    // Target & Module
    "target": "ES2023",
    "lib": ["ES2023"],
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",

    // Module Interop
    "allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,

    // Strictness
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": false,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,

    // Output
    "sourceMap": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true
  }
}
```

### Notes on TypeScript Configuration

- **Module system**: Uses `NodeNext` for both `module` and `moduleResolution` - this is the modern approach for Node.js projects and works well with ESM
- **Strictness**: Full strict mode enabled with additional checks like `noImplicitReturns` and `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`
- **`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`**: Deliberately set to `false` - while safer when `true`, it often creates excessive noise

### Project-Specific Settings to Add

These settings should be customized per project:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src",
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": {}
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*.ts"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}
```

---

## Prettier Configuration

### .prettierrc.json Template

```json
{
  "semi": true,
  "trailingComma": "all",
  "singleQuote": true,
  "printWidth": 100,
  "tabWidth": 2,
  "useTabs": false,
  "endOfLine": "lf",
  "arrowParens": "always",
  "bracketSpacing": true
}
```

### .prettierignore Template

```
node_modules
dist
coverage
.vscode
.idea
*.lock
package-lock.json
yarn.lock
pnpm-lock.yaml
```

**Note**: Add project-specific paths as needed (e.g., generated code directories, vendor files).

---

## Package Manager: pnpm

Use pnpm for all Node.js projects unless otherwise specified.

### Initial Setup Commands

```bash
# Initialize new project
pnpm init

# Install dependencies
pnpm add <package>

# Install dev dependencies
pnpm add -D <package>

# Common dev dependencies for TypeScript projects
pnpm add -D typescript @types/node prettier
```

### pnpm Workspace Setup (for monorepos)

Create `pnpm-workspace.yaml`:

```yaml
packages:
  - 'packages/*'
  - 'apps/*'
```

---

## Quick Start Checklist

When setting up a new Node.js/TypeScript project:

1. **Initialize project**: `pnpm init`
2. **Install TypeScript**: `pnpm add -D typescript @types/node`
3. **Create tsconfig.json**: Use the template above
4. **Install Prettier**: `pnpm add -D prettier`
5. **Create .prettierrc.json**: Use the template above
6. **Create .prettierignore**: Use the template above
7. **Create src/ directory**: `mkdir src`
8. **Create entry point**: `touch src/index.ts`
9. **Add scripts to package.json**:
   ```json
   {
     "scripts": {
       "build": "tsc",
       "dev": "tsc --watch",
       "format": "prettier --write .",
       "format:check": "prettier --check ."
     }
   }
   ```

---

## User Invocation

This skill provides context when setting up new projects. It can be referenced:

- When asking to create a new project
- When setting up TypeScript configuration
- When configuring prettier
- When initializing a new Node.js project

The preferences in this skill should be applied automatically when creating new projects unless the user specifies different preferences.

# The screen catalog

One Markdown file per Frame Job screen: how to reach it, what to capture, and a
description of it for someone who has never seen the app — the text a design
request carries beside the pictures. `tools/proof/screens.py` reads every file
here, drives its own Frame Job into each screen over MCP and the dev tools, and
writes the PNGs (light and dark) and one `screens.md` pairing each picture with
its prose into `tools/proof/work/screens/<date>/`. The prose lives here so it
changes with the screens; the pictures are made fresh each run and are not kept
in the repository.

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py            # the whole catalog; tools/proof/README.md has the rest
```

## A screen file

The file's first non-blank line is ```` ```json screen ````; the block ends at
the next line that is exactly ```` ``` ````. What is between is one JSON object,
the front block. Everything after the closing fence is the prose, copied into
`screens.md` verbatim. The file's name without `.md` is the screen's id, and the
screens run in name order.

```json
{
  "title": "Clip inspector — Sound",
  "project": "demo",
  "steps": [
    {"call": "set_selection", "args": {"clips": ["$clip:tone"]}},
    {"call": "set_playhead", "args": {"t": 1500000}}
  ],
  "captures": [
    {"name": "window", "window": "editor"},
    {"name": "inspector", "window": "editor", "view": "inspector"}
  ],
  "after": [],
  "expect": [{"capture": "inspector", "visible_text": "Gain"}]
}
```

- `title` (required): the heading in `screens.md`.
- `project` (required): `null` (no project open — Welcome, Settings), `"empty"`
  or `"demo"`, a fixture `screens.py` builds (below). It is opened before the
  steps run.

# Handoff: Reelcut — sharp chrome

> **Scope: Reelcut only** (`kpgalligan/reelcut`, AppKit in `app/Sources/`).
> Everything in this folder is about the Reelcut editor window. A separate handoff exists for Rasterize. It is not referenced here and none of its parts belong in this codebase. Do **not** add a tool rail, options bar, layers panel, assistant panel, status bar or zoom HUD to Reelcut.
> *Amended 2026-09-27 by spec §11 AI-4 (road map 12): the Assistant is the inspector's fourth tab, never a panel of its own; the rest of this line stands.*

## Overview

This visual pass follows on from the existing chrome-cleanup handoff (`designs/design_handoff_chrome/`). That handoff's layout, regions, clusters, metrics and behaviour stay as specified. This one changes three things:

1. **Corners.** Every chrome component goes square (0 radius). Timeline clips are the one exception and take **2pt**.
2. **Slider knob.** The zoom slider's round 11pt knob becomes a 7 × 11pt block.
3. **Light appearance.** Reference values are provided so both appearances can be checked. In AppKit, keep the semantic `DS` colours; they already follow the system appearance.

No core (Rust) changes are needed.

## About the design files

`design/` holds **design references built in HTML**: a clickable prototype of the Reelcut editor. It is not production code to port. Recreate it in AppKit with the repo's existing patterns: self-drawing `NSView` subclasses, `DS` tokens in `Theme.swift`, and `GhostButton`, `AccentButton`, `PanelTabsView`, `DSField` and `DividerView` in `Controls.swift`. Ship SF Symbols. The Material Symbols font in the HTML is only a browser stand-in.

`design/runtime/ds_bundle.js` is a compiled browser runtime that lets the prototype render. It comes from a shared web library that also contains components for another app. **Do not read it, port it, or treat any name in it as a Reelcut requirement.** The Reelcut component list is the one below.

## Fidelity

**High fidelity.** Colours, type and metrics are final. Dark appearance is authoritative; light is reference (see *Design tokens*).

## Screen: Editor window (1440 × 862 content)

```
title bar 30  ─ traffic lights · centred "Untitled Project" + mono meta
toolbar 44    ─ transport ×6 · | · timecode ——— Fit popup · Safe ☐ · | · Export
preview well (flex) ─────────────────────────────┬─ inspector 304
                                                 │  tabs 32: Clip · Media · Document
timeline bar 36 ─ selection block · | · edit ×7 · | · Snap ☑ ——— zoom slider · | · S M L
ruler 22 ─ track headers 132 │ lanes
```

### Radius changes (the core of this handoff)

| Element | Current | New |
|---|---|---|
| `DS.controlRadius` (fields, checkboxes, segmented cells, popups) | 3 | **0** |
| `DS.buttonRadius` (AccentButton/Export, GhostButton hover fill, bordered buttons) | 4 | **0** |
| `GhostButton(cornerRadius:)` default | 8 | **0** |
| `DS.listRowRadius` (Media tab rows) | 5 | **0** |
| `DS.fieldRadius` (`DSField` legacy fields) | 7 | **0** |
| Timecode field | 4 | **0** |
| Media thumbnail (34 × 38) | 3 | **0** |
| Kind chips (8 × 20 / 8 × 26) and the 6 × 6 track dot | 2 / 1 | **0** |
| S/M/L segmented end cells | 3 | **0** |

export const meta = {
  name: 'framejob-feature-inventory',
  description: 'Sweep guide, code and history for every Frame Job feature; build a page taxonomy; merge and reconcile',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Sweep', detail: 'one agent per guide page and per code lens, each blind to the others' },
    { title: 'Taxonomy', detail: 'design the site structure from all raw records' },
    { title: 'Merge', detail: 'per-section dedupe of raw records into canonical features' },
    { title: 'Reconcile', detail: 'orphans, duplicates, final features.json' },
  ],
}

const S = args.scratch
const REPO = args.repo

const AREAS = 'interface, projects, media, timeline, playback, editing, canvas, text-shapes, effects, mattes, motion, transitions, speed, audio, cleanup, captions, transcript, color, hdr, graphics, framing, multicam, recording, export, assistant, mcp, settings, other'

const COMMON = `You are helping build the public user documentation site for Frame Job, a native macOS video editor. The repo is at ${REPO} (your working directory). Read-only: do not modify anything in the repo. Your only output file goes under ${S}/inventory/.

The job right now is an EXHAUSTIVE inventory of every feature of the app as it exists in this tree.

What counts as a feature: anything a user can do, see, choose or rely on in the shipped app — each menu command, tool, gesture, inspector section, control group, sheet, option that changes behaviour, supported file format, preset, automatic behaviour the user would notice, each MCP tool. Go fine-grained: a section with 8 distinct controls is one record per control that has its own behaviour, not one record for the section. Prefer too many records to too few; dedupe happens later.

What does NOT count: internals with no visible effect, and anything dev-only — tools or code behind FRAMEJOB_DEV_TOOLS (snapshot_ui, perform_menu_item, cancel_sheet, select_inspector_tab, play_preview, graphic_memory, loudness_meter, land_recording, analysis_job, transcript_view, playback_rebuilds, assistant_send, assistant_answer), -RCDev* launch defaults, tools/proof. Also nothing deferred, not wanted, or not built: the tree is the authority, so a feature in a design document that the code does not have is not a feature.

Write a JSON array to the file named below, one object per feature:
{"id":"<lens>-001","name":"short user-facing name","area":"<one of: ${AREAS}>","what":"one plain sentence: what the user gets","ui":["where it lives, with the shortcut, e.g. Clip ▸ Split (⌘T)"],"mcp":["agent tool names, if known"],"requires":["anthropic-key | assemblyai-key | macos-permission:<what> | on-device-model | none"],"details":["options, limits, defaults, refusal rules worth documenting"],"evidence":"file:line or guide page and heading"}

Ids are sequential with your lens name as the prefix. "mcp" and "requires" can be empty arrays. Write valid JSON (check it with: python3 -m json.tool <file> >/dev/null). Then return only the file path, the record count and any notes on what you could not cover.`

const FINDER = { type: 'object', properties: { file: { type: 'string' }, count: { type: 'number' }, notes: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['file', 'count'] }

const GUIDE_PAGES = ['projects-and-media', 'timeline', 'editing', 'canvas-and-layers', 'motion-and-transitions', 'speed', 'audio', 'cleanup-tools', 'captions', 'transcript', 'color-grading', 'hdr-and-color', 'graphics', 'vertical-and-framing', 'multicam', 'screen-recording', 'export', 'assistant', 'mcp', 'settings', 'menus-and-shortcuts']

const guideLenses = GUIDE_PAGES.map(p => ({
  lens: 'guide-' + p,
  effort: 'medium',
  prompt: `${COMMON}

Your lens: the user guide page docs/guide/${p}.md. Read the whole page and extract every feature it describes, section by section, with its details. Every heading, every bulleted option and every named control should be accounted for. Output file: ${S}/inventory/raw/guide-${p}.json`,
}))

const CODE_RULE = `Your lens reads the CODE. Do NOT read docs/guide/ or README.md: the point of this lens is to catch what the guide misses. app/CLAUDE.md has the Swift file map, core/CLAUDE.md the Rust module map. app/Sources has 827 Swift files, so grep and list first, then read.`

const codeLenses = [
  { lens: 'code-menus', prompt: `Every menu in the menu bar and every context menu: start at app/Sources/AppDelegate+Menus*.swift, then grep NSMenuItem and NSMenu across app/Sources for right-click and pop-up menus (timeline clip, track header, ruler, marker, media row, preview, inspector). One record per item (submenus' leaves too) with its exact title, key equivalent and the condition that enables it. Skip items behind FRAMEJOB_DEV_TOOLS.` },
  { lens: 'code-clip-inspector', prompt: `The Clip tab of the inspector: start at ClipPane.makeSections() and read every registered section. One record per control or control group with its own behaviour: every slider, popup, checkbox, button and sub-tab, with ranges and defaults. Include sections that appear only for one clip kind (video, audio, text, shape, image, background, graphic, adjustment, matte, nest).` },
  { lens: 'code-other-panes', prompt: `Everything in the window that is not the Clip tab: the Media tab, Document tab, Transcript tab, Assistant tab, Color tab if separate, the toolbar and transport, the preview well and its overlays (safe areas, scopes, subjects, handles), the timeline bar, track headers, ruler, status and meter displays, the title bar, Welcome window. One record per control or display with its own behaviour.` },
  { lens: 'code-gestures', prompt: `Direct manipulation and keys with no menu item: the gesture session structs and mouse handling in the timeline and preview (drag, trim, slip, roll, rate stretch, marquee, zoom about the cursor, snapping modifiers, band drags on the action lane, crop and transform handles on the preview, drag and drop from Finder and from the Media tab), and keyDown/performKeyEquivalent handling (J/K/L, arrows, typed timecode, and so on). One record per gesture or key with its modifiers.` },
  { lens: 'code-sheets', prompt: `Every sheet, dialog, panel and secondary window: grep beginSheet, NSPanel, NSWindow subclasses, *Sheet*.swift and *Panel*.swift. For each one, list every field with its default, what the primary button does and what refuses it. Include Settings and every pane within it, the Export sheet, the Export Queue, the recorder panel, Remove Silences, Remove Filler Words, Generate Captions, Speed, Speed Ramp, Retime Range, Auto Zoom, Speed Up Typing, Follow Subject, Make Vertical, Switch by Speaker, Match Audio, Synchronize Audio, the graphic browser, Import Graphic, and any other you find.` },
  { lens: 'code-mcp-catalog', prompt: `Every tool an agent can call: read app/Sources/AgentCatalog*.swift and list every tool with its purpose, arguments and refusal rules. Exclude the dev tools named above. Also the connection story: the agent socket, framejob-mcp in Contents/Helpers (mcp-proxy/), Copy MCP Command, what launches the app, the scope envelope key.` },
  { lens: 'code-core-ops', prompt: `Every edit op in the Rust core: core/src/edit.rs's module-doc table and core/src/op_table.rs. One record per op with what it means to a user, its arguments and its refusals. Map to the UI path if you can see it from the op's Swift builder in app/Sources/ReelOps.swift.` },
  { lens: 'code-formats', prompt: `Every file format and codec the app reads or writes: import (movies, sound, pictures, WebM and MKV, camera log formats, caption formats, LUTs, fonts, graphics packages), export rows (core export settings, ExportSettings, codecs, containers, audio formats, frame sizes, frame rates, presets, HDR deliverables, alpha, stems, still frames, captions), the .framejob package and its layout, recording output. One record per format or preset with limits.` },
  { lens: 'code-analysis-ai', prompt: `Everything Frame Job works out from the media, or asks a service: on-device analysis (Vision, Sound Analysis, Silero VAD, Speech, person segmentation, faces, saliency, shots, foreground masks), cached analysis, on-device transcription, AssemblyAI cloud transcription, the Anthropic-backed Assistant, ModelKeys, the spend ledger and pricing display, permission prompts (camera, microphone, screen recording), what leaves the machine and what does not, Sparkle updates. One record per user-visible behaviour.` },
  { lens: 'code-graphics', prompt: `The motion graphics engine as a user sees it: graphic/ (the Module API), docs/graphics-api.md, every bundled graphic template (find the bundled list and name each one with its properties), the graphic browser, per-graphic inspector properties, fonts and assets, versions and restore, import and export of graphic packages, Background render, the graphic reference for agents.` },
  { lens: 'code-color', prompt: `Colour as a user sees it: the Color tab and its sub-tabs, tone controls, wheels, curves (RGB, Hue vs Hue, Hue vs Sat and the rest), qualifiers, looks (name each bundled look), .cube LUTs, adjustment clips, Show Ungraded, Show Selection, every scope and its options, HDR working spaces, deliverables, Show SDR Version, canvas.blending, camera log and media colour (each supported log profile), HDR-to-SDR conversion. One record per control.` },
  { lens: 'code-audio', prompt: `Audio as a user sees it: every clip audio control and processor (EQ, hum, channels, gate, de-esser, leveller, voice isolation, de-reverb, voice effects, Enhance Voice), Normalize, loudness meter, volume line, fades and shapes, J and L cuts, track volume, pan, compressor, limiter, stems, ducking, Match Audio, Synchronize Audio, scrub audio, sample rates and master. One record per control, with ranges and defaults.` },
  { lens: 'code-recording', prompt: `Recording as a user sees it: the recorder panel, screen, window, picked-window, camera, microphone, system audio, click rings, the cursor modes (Separate and In the picture), pause and resume, voice-over recording, Enhance when a recording lands, the camera layout, Clip ▸ Camera Layout, cursor tracks, Auto Zoom, shortcut overlays, Speed Up Typing, what recording writes. One record per control or behaviour.` },
  { lens: 'code-roadmaps', prompt: `The design record of what shipped: designs/creator-jobs.md (a road map still in progress: check the tree for each item, include only what the code has) and every file in designs/adr/ (condensed records of closed work; skip file-history records). One record per user-visible feature each describes. Confirm each exists by grepping app/Sources or core/src, and drop those deferred or not wanted. This lens may read designs/, not docs/guide/.` },
  { lens: 'code-history', prompt: `Git history: read the subjects of the last 400 commits (git log --format=%s -400). They are long and descriptive. List every user-visible feature or behaviour they name, then confirm each one by grepping the tree. This lens catches recent work that the documents may not mention yet, so mark the most recent ones carefully.` },
  { lens: 'code-screens', prompt: `The screen catalog: designs/screens/*.md, one per screen, with a designer-facing description. Read them all and list every control, panel and region each describes as a feature record. Also read designs/spec/09* (keys and menus) from designs/spec/README.md's index, and add every key or menu it names that the tree still has.` },
].map(l => ({ ...l, effort: 'high', prompt: `${COMMON}\n\n${CODE_RULE}\n\nYour lens (${l.lens}): ${l.prompt}\n\nOutput file: ${S}/inventory/raw/${l.lens}.json` }))

phase('Sweep')
const sweep = await parallel([...guideLenses, ...codeLenses].map(l => () =>
  agent(l.prompt, { label: l.lens, phase: 'Sweep', schema: FINDER, effort: l.effort })
    .then(r => r ? { lens: l.lens, ...r } : null)))
const ok = sweep.filter(Boolean)
log(`Sweep: ${ok.length} of ${guideLenses.length + codeLenses.length} lenses, ${ok.reduce((a, r) => a + r.count, 0)} raw records`)
const failed = [...guideLenses, ...codeLenses].map(l => l.lens).filter(n => !ok.find(r => r.lens === n))
if (failed.length) log('Lenses with no result: ' + failed.join(', '))

phase('Taxonomy')
const TAX = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    file: { type: 'string' },
    pages: { type: 'number' },
    sections: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string' }, title: { type: 'string' }, pages: { type: 'number' } }, required: ['id', 'title', 'pages'] } },
  },
  required: ['file', 'pages', 'sections'],
}
const taxonomy = await agent(`You are the information architect for the public user documentation site of Frame Job, a native macOS video editor. The repo is your working directory (${REPO}); read-only. A sweep has written raw feature records into ${S}/inventory/raw/*.json (fields: id, name, area, what, ui, mcp, requires, details, evidence). Guide-page lenses are guide-*.json; code lenses are code-*.json. Use jq or python to read name and what across all of them; read docs/guide/README.md for the existing page order.

Design the site's structure and write it to ${S}/inventory/taxonomy.json:
{"sections":[{"id":"timeline","title":"Timeline and playback","order":4,"summary":"one sentence","areas":["timeline","playback"],"pages":[{"slug":"timeline/markers","title":"Markers","order":6,"kind":"feature|concept|howto|reference|overview","scope":"one or two sentences: exactly what this page covers and where its edges are","guide":["docs/guide/timeline.md#markers"]}]}]}

Rules for the structure:
- A reader looks a feature up by the name of what they want to do. A page covers ONE feature or one tight family of features (for example "Trimming", "Markers", "Noise reduction"). No catch-all pages, and no page so broad it needs more than about 300 lines. Split a guide page wherever it covers several independently useful things. Err towards more, smaller pages.
- Every raw record must have an obvious home page. A feature used in two places has one primary page.
- Section order follows the way someone learns the app: Getting started; Projects and media; Timeline and playback; Editing; Canvas and layers; text, shapes and pictures; Effects and keying; Motion and transitions; Speed; Audio; Clean-up tools; Captions and transcript; Colour; HDR and colour management; Motion graphics; Vertical and framing; Multicam; Recording; Export; the Assistant; Agents and MCP; Reference. Adjust where the records argue for it, and sub-group a section only by slug prefix depth of one (section/page).
- Getting started needs: requirements and install, your first edit, a tour of the editor window, core concepts, undo and saving, a page on the AI features and bringing your own keys (what is optional, what stays on the Mac).
- Reference needs: all menus, keyboard shortcuts, gestures with no menu item, settings, supported file formats, the .framejob package, a glossary, a troubleshooting page drawn only from the refusals and limits recorded in the code and guide.
- Agents and MCP needs a tool reference grouped by concern, one page per group, covering every tool.
- Motion graphics needs a page listing each bundled template, and a pointer to the module API.
- Slugs: lowercase kebab, section-id/page-id. Use American spelling in slugs (color not colour) so URLs match the app's own labels, and "Color" for UI labels, but the docs' prose follows docs/guide (colour).
- Do not include a page for anything dev-only or unbuilt.

Return the file path, the page count and the section list.`, { label: 'taxonomy', phase: 'Taxonomy', schema: TAX })

log(`Taxonomy: ${taxonomy.pages} pages in ${taxonomy.sections.length} sections`)

phase('Merge')
const MERGED = { type: 'object', properties: { file: { type: 'string' }, features: { type: 'number' }, rejected: { type: 'number' }, empty_pages: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } } }, required: ['file', 'features', 'rejected'] }
const merged = await parallel(taxonomy.sections.map(sec => () => agent(`You are merging raw feature records for ONE section of the Frame Job documentation site. Repo: ${REPO} (your working directory, read-only). Raw records: ${S}/inventory/raw/*.json. Taxonomy: ${S}/inventory/taxonomy.json. Your section: id "${sec.id}" ("${sec.title}").

Go through ALL raw records: use each record's area, its ui and its name, and keyword-search the others too, since a record tagged with another area may belong to one of your pages. For each page in your section, produce the canonical features: dedupe across lenses (guide lenses and code lenses describe the same thing in different words). — but it is the obvious way to get a frame-numbered test card):

```sh
mkdir -p tools/proof/media && cd tools/proof/media
ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "testsrc=size=640x360:rate=30:duration=10"  -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:v libx264 A.mov

```

Phase 2 adds sound. The three movies above are silent, and a clip of a
silent movie has NO audio group (an `.m4a` clip has no video group), so the
solo proof needs two tones it can tell apart by ear and by byte, and the
paste-attributes proof needs one clip that has BOTH groups:

```sh
ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=440:sample_rate=48000:duration=5" -ac 2 -c:a aac -b:a 128k toneA.m4a
ffmpeg -y -f lavfi -i "sine=frequency=880:sample_rate=48000:duration=5" -ac 2 -c:a aac -b:a 128k toneB.m4a
```

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, Node is pinned by `.node-version`. `README.md` has the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             the section order; each section autogenerates from its folder
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx, ordered by `sidebar.order`
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over `docs/guide/`, a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose, as `docs/guide/` does (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Timeline ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension, and `narrow` keeps an inspector capture from filling the column. Use a screen only
  when it shows what the page is about, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here as well as `docs/guide/`, and a new feature adds its row
to `src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, or a
page that names something internal.

360:## Markers
## Markers

Markers are flags on the ruler at project time. A **chapter marker** is
drawn as a filled flag and also becomes a chapter in exported movies (see
[Export](export.md)); an ordinary marker is an outline.

| To | Do this |
|---|---|
| Add a marker at the playhead | M, the bookmark button in the timeline bar, or **Mark ▸ Add Marker** |
| Move one | Drag its flag along the ruler (it snaps) |
| Rename one | Double-click its flag, or type in its row in the Document tab |
| Make it a chapter | Tick **Chapter** in its Document-tab row |
| Jump to one | **Mark ▸ Next Marker** / **Previous Marker**, or **Go** in its Document-tab row |
| Remove one | **Delete** in its Document-tab row |

The Document tab's **Markers** section lists every marker in time order with
its time, its name, **Chapter**, **Go** and **Delete**. With none it says
"No markers. Press M to add one."

A new marker is called `Marker N` and is red. Two markers can't share a frame,
so M on a frame that already has a marker beeps, and a drag onto another
marker's frame doesn't move it. **Next Marker** and **Previous Marker** pause
playback and jump; they beep when there is no marker further in that
direction, and are dimmed when the project has no markers.

Markers belong to the whole timeline. While a nest is open the ruler shows no
markers and drags don't snap to them, the three Mark ▸ marker commands are
off (a bare M beeps), and **Go** is disabled (the playhead inside a nest
counts from the nest's own start). The Document tab's Markers list still
shows every marker, and its name field, **Chapter** and **Delete** still
work.

A marker's colour is set only through an agent. The names are the six label
colours (below); any other name draws in the neutral text colour.

*Agents:* `add_marker {at?, name?, chapter?, color?}` (at the playhead when
`at` is left out), `set_marker {marker, time?, name?, chapter?, color?}`,
`remove_marker {marker}`.

input.content:
---
title: Markers
description: Flag moments on the timeline, name them, jump between them, and turn them into chapters in an exported movie.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

A marker is a flag on the ruler that remembers a moment in the project: a beat to cut on, a line to come back to, the start of a chapter.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['Mark ▸ Add Marker', 'Mark ▸ Next Marker', 'Mark ▸ Previous Marker']}
  keys="M"
  where={['The bookmark button in the timeline bar', 'Document tab ▸ Markers']}
  tools={['add_marker', 'set_marker', 'remove_marker']}
/>

## Add a marker

Move the playhead to the moment and press <kbd>M</kbd>. The bookmark button in the timeline bar and **Mark ▸ Add Marker** do the same.

A new marker is red and is called `Marker 1`, `Marker 2` and so on. Two markers can't share a frame, so pressing <kbd>M</kbd> on a frame that already has one beeps and adds nothing.

## Move, rename and remove a marker

| To | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Move a marker | Drag its flag along the ruler. It snaps, and it won't land on a frame that already has a marker. |
| Rename a marker | Double-click its flag, or type in its row in the Document tab. |
| Remove a marker | Choose **Delete** in its row in the Document tab. |

## Jump between markers

**Mark ▸ Next Marker** and **Mark ▸ Previous Marker** pause playback and move the playhead to the marker. They beep when there's no marker further in that direction, and they're dimmed when the project has no markers.

You can also choose **Go** in a marker's row in the Document tab.

## The Markers list

The **Markers** section of the [Document tab](/projects/document-tab/) lists every marker in time order, with its time, its name, **Chapter**, **Go** and **Delete**. With no markers it reads "No markers. Press M to add one."

<Shot
  name="11-document-inspector.inspector"
  alt="The Document tab of the inspector, showing the project's canvas settings."
  narrow
/>

## Make a chapter

Tick **Chapter** in a marker's row. A chapter marker draws as a filled flag, and an ordinary marker as an outline.

Chapter markers become chapters in exported MP4, MOV, M4A and WebM files, in time order. A chapter takes the marker's name, or "Chapter 1", "Chapter 2" and so on when the marker has no name. See [Chapters](/export/chapters/) for how a range export treats them.

## Marker colours

A marker's colour can only be set by an agent, with `add_marker` or `set_marker`. The colour names are the six [clip label](/timeline/clip-labels/) colours, and any other name draws the marker in the neutral text colour.

## Good to know

Markers belong to the whole timeline, not to a nest. While a [nest](/editing/nests/) is open:

- The ruler shows no markers, and drags don't snap to them.
- The three marker commands in the **Mark** menu are off, and pressing <kbd>M</kbd> beeps.
- **Go** is disabled, because the playhead inside a nest counts from the nest's own start.
- The Document tab's list still shows every marker, and its name field, **Chapter** and **Delete** still work.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
- [The in and out range](/timeline/in-out-range/)
- [Chapters](/export/chapters/)

     A stretch no longer than twice this value is not cut.
     After this comes the snap to the frame grid, so a frame more of room tone can remain.
     Raise it if a word is clipped.
     Agent argument: padding in ticks, default 60000, from 0 to 9,000,000,000,000,000. It is not snapped to frames and not held to the sheet's range.

## Remove Silences

**Clip ▸ Remove Silences…** opens the Remove Silences sheet. The command is available whenever the timeline has a clip whose sound is switched on.

### What "silent" means

Silence is measured in the **mix**, as you hear it, not in the raw file:

- A clip you have turned down, faded out, ducked, muted, or silenced by soloing another track is quiet. It never keeps a cut from happening.
- A stretch where *every* clip in scope is quiet counts as silent. A music bed under a voice-over therefore keeps the pauses in the speech from being cut, unless you limit the scope to the voice clip (see **In:** below).
- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording; it does not close the gaps you placed between clips. **Clip ▸ Close Gap** does that.
- A muted clip is left out of the analysis entirely. A muted music bed is never read as one long silence covering the whole song.

### Judge by Voice or Level

**Judge by:** picks how a moment is tested.

| Mode | What counts as quiet | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Voice | Nobody is talking. An on-device voice-activity model listens to each media file once and keeps its answer with the project. A quiet microphone isn't mistaken for silence, and a hum isn't mistaken for speech. | Yes |
| Level | The sound in the mix is quieter than the threshold. | Used when the voice model can't be used |

In Voice mode, a clip with no voice in it at all, such as music or a tone, is judged by level instead. The sheet names each such clip, for example "Intro music at 00:00:12:00 holds no voice and is judged by level." That is why, in Voice mode, the threshold row is labelled **Level if no voice:**.

If the voice model can't be used on this Mac, the sheet opens in Level mode with Voice greyed out and says "The voice model could not be used, so quiet is judged by level." This lasts until you relaunch Frame Job.

Voice analysis runs on your Mac. Nothing is uploaded.

### The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Judge by:** | Voice or Level, as above. | Voice | n/a |
| **Quieter than:** (Level mode) / **Level if no voice:** (Voice mode) | A slider in whole dBFS, with the value shown beside it. In Level mode, sound at or below it is quiet. In Voice mode, it judges clips that hold no voice, and a clip the mix turns down below it is quiet whatever it contains. | −40 dBFS | −80 to −10 dBFS |
| **Longer than:** | The shortest quiet stretch worth cutting, in seconds. Shorter pauses, such as the gap between two words, are kept. | 0.5 s | 0.05 to 10 s |
| **Keep at ends:** | How much of each quiet stretch to keep at each end, in seconds, so speech doesn't start or end abruptly. A stretch shorter than twice this value is not cut. | 0.1 s | 0 to 2 s |
| **In:** | **Selected clips** analyses only the selected clips. **All audible clips** analyses everything you can hear. | Selected clips when the selection includes something audible, otherwise All audible clips | n/a |

**Selected clips** is greyed out when nothing selected makes a sound. A number outside a field's range is refused: the field keeps the text and won't accept it, and **Remove** beeps, until you type a number inside the range (0.05–10 s for **Longer than:**, 0–2 s for **Keep at ends:**). The count and the shading update as you change any control.

---
title: Remove Silences
description: Find the dead air in a spoken recording, see it on the timeline, and cut it all as one edit.
---

import { Steps } from '@components/starlight';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Remove Silences finds the dead air in a spoken recording, shows you what it would cut, and takes it all out as one undo step, closing the timeline over each cut.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Remove Silences…"
  tools={['detect_silence', 'ripple_delete_ranges']}
  needs="Nothing. Voice detection runs on your Mac, with no key and no upload."
/>

## Remove the silences

<Steps>

1. Choose **Clip ▸ Remove Silences…**. It's available when the timeline has a clip with its sound on. If there turns out to be nothing to measure, Frame Job beeps instead of opening the sheet.

2. Check what's shaded on the timeline, and read the count in the sheet. Both update as you change a control.

3. Adjust the [controls](#the-controls) until the cuts look right.

4. Choose **Remove**.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="14-remove-silences-sheet.sheet"
  alt="The Remove Silences sheet, with Judge by set to Voice, a Level if no voice slider at −40 dBFS, Longer than 0.5 seconds, Keep at ends 0.1 seconds, and In set to All audible clips."
/>

The sheet opens on its defaults every time. It doesn't remember your last settings.

## The controls

| Control | What it does | Default | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Judge by:** | How a moment is tested. See [What counts as silent](/cleanup/voice-or-level/). | Voice | Voice, Level |
| **Quieter than:** or **Level if no voice:** | The level that counts as quiet. The row reads **Quieter than:** in Level mode and **Level if no voice:** in Voice mode. | −40 dBFS | −80 to −10 dBFS |
| **Longer than:** | The shortest quiet stretch worth cutting. Shorter pauses, such as the gap between two words, stay. | 0.5 s | 0.05 to 10 s |
| **Keep at ends:** | How much of each quiet stretch to keep at each end, so speech doesn't start or stop abruptly. | 0.1 s | 0 to 2 s |
| **In:** | Whether to look at **Selected clips** or **All audible clips**. | Selected clips when the selection has something audible, otherwise All audible clips | |

**Selected clips** is greyed out when nothing selected makes a sound, and a selection of muted clips counts as nothing audible. Choose it to stop a music bed under a voice-over from holding the cuts up.

**Longer than:** measures the stretch as you hear it, before **Keep at ends:** takes its share. A stretch no longer than twice **Keep at ends:** isn't cut. Cuts then snap to the frame grid, so a frame more of room tone can remain. Raise **Keep at ends:** if a word gets clipped.

The two number fields take up to two decimal places. A number outside the range stays in the field and **Remove** beeps until you fix it.

## What the sheet tells you

The sheet explains itself under the count. It can show more than one of these at once.

| The sheet says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Nothing in this timeline is audible, so nothing was analysed." | Nothing in scope makes a sound. With **Selected clips** it reads "Nothing the selected clips play is audible in the mix, so nothing was analysed." |
| "The waveform is still being analysed for …" or "Speech is still being analysed for …" | Frame Job hasn't finished with those files, which often happens straight after an import. Leave the sheet open and it updates as each one lands. |
| "Quiet inside a nest is left alone…" | A nest held enough quiet to have been cut, so a low count doesn't mean there's no dead air. Open the nest with <kbd>⌘↓</kbd> and remove its silences there. |

Relinking a file starts its analysis again. An open sheet drops the old answers at once and updates when the new ones land.

## Good to know

- A gap with nothing audible in it is left alone. Remove Silences takes dead air out of a recording, not the gaps you placed between clips. [Close Gap](/editing/close-gaps/) does that.
- Nothing inside a [nest](/editing/nests/) is cut, because a nest plays from its first frame and a cut into one would strand the rest of it.
- A quiet stretch broken up by a nest or a transition is measured in its pieces.

## With an agent

`detect_silence` reads the same ranges the sheet would cut and changes nothing. Pass them to `ripple_delete_ranges` to make the cut. See [Tools: clean-up](/mcp/tools-clean-up/).

## Related

- [What counts as silent](/cleanup/voice-or-level/)
- [How a clean-up cut works](/cleanup/how-cleanup-cuts-work/)
- [Remove Filler Words](/cleanup/remove-filler-words/)
